item.title: AHEADance: Anticipatory Humanoid Dance from Streaming Audio
item.description: arXiv:2611.13370v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A humanoid that dances to streamed music must commit each motion chunk before it has heard the music that chunk accompanies, and must continue from motion it has already committed. We present AHEADance, a robot-native streaming dance generator executed on a humanoid robot by a whole-body tracker. ListenAhead conditions each chunk on heard music and a frozen music model's forecasts of the coming music, aligned to their target times and weighted by reliability. The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future; with them, the generator is better synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at its song's beat frequency. Commit Forcing trains continuation from the model's own committed chunks, updating both the latent history and the decoded boundary of the next chunk; it reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%, the level of real dance. Three music evaluators, each validated on real G1 dance, test synchronization, song and style. On a physical Unitree G1, it dances while the music plays and comes to rest when it stops, without a fall. Project page: https://ihcr.github.io/AHEADance
item.dc:creator: Tianhu Peng, Yukun Wang, Lingfan Bao, Yiyang Jia, Chengxu Zhou

item.title: Complete Decentralization of Wave Equation Control on a Compact Domain
item.description: arXiv:2611.13449v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A feedback control policy is completely decentralized if the actuation signal at each location in space can be computed based only on state information from that location. For systems equipped with large numbers of spatially distributed sensors and actuators, completely decentralized controllers are desirable since they can be implemented in a communication and computation efficient manner, but generally perform worse than centralized counterparts. However, through a case study of Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) design for wave dynamics on a compact spatial domain, we show that careful design of system parameters to satisfy certain conditions causes a decentralized control policy to perform as well as any centralized policy. We then propose a spatially filtered $H_2$ norm to show that satisfying these conditions does not inherently degrade achievable closed-loop system performance, enabling simultaneous realization of both desirable performance and communication/computation efficiency via system-control co-design. Additional robustness analysis characterizes a range of system parameters such that the system interconnected with a decentralized controller maintains stability and near-optimal performance. Although our framework is derived for spatially continuous dynamics, we demonstrate that this theory can be leveraged to derive results for decentralization in finite-dimensional settings through a damped mass-spring example.
item.dc:creator: Addie McCurdy, Emily Jensen

item.title: Metamorphic testing of learned AC optimal power flow surrogates reveals representation dependence
item.description: arXiv:2611.13566v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluating a learned AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF) surrogate on one grid serialization cannot show whether its accuracy depends on that encoding. We test this dependence with thirteen metamorphic relations, each specifying when a transformation is valid and how to compare its outputs. Our audit covers 17 model and pipeline configurations: two released trained checkpoints and 15 random-weight architecture or mechanism controls. Every configuration violates at least six relations, even at reporting tolerances ten times tighter or looser. For GridSFM-Open v1.1, source inspection and intermediate-tensor interventions point to an indexing bug and three noncanonical or numerically unstable preprocessing choices; a repaired checkpoint remains untested. In a separate case500 training experiment, augmentation lowers transformed-view error in three of four models and median discrepancy and constraint-violation P95 in all four. These benefits depend on the training protocol: some relations worsen, and every evaluated prediction remains AC infeasible. A GPU/CPU eigensolver mismatch accounts for most of the large raw-Laplacian-baseline gain. We recommend reporting representation consistency alongside accuracy, feasibility, and cost. These results establish neither deployment readiness nor universal invariance.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Peng, Vineet Jagadeesan Nair

item.title: Toward Pseudorange-Based PNT with Starlink: A Mock Fused LEO GNSS Implementation
item.description: arXiv:2611.13655v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present experimental results from Starlink for pseudorange-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), emulating a system that fuses a primary communications mission with a secondary low-Earth orbit (LEO) PNT mission. Legacy global navigation satellite system (GNSS) constellations faceinherent vulnerabilities and signal limitations, prompting growing interest in broadband LEO constellations---such as SpaceX's Starlink---for resilient PNT. However, opportunistic use of stand-alone Starlink signals fails to achieve GNSS-competitive accuracy due to frame timing irregularities and reliance on uncorrected poor-quality publicly available ephemeris data. To overcome these limitations, we present a mock implementation of a fused LEO GNSS architecture. Our method extracts time-of-arrival observables from live Starlink Ku-band downlinks and pairs them with high-fidelity, beam-specific orbit and clock models distributed as if provided natively by the constellation operator. In a field campaign, and despite constraints imposed by consumer-grade receiver hardware, the method yields 95% error bounds of 2.33 m horizontally (semi-major axis), 3.37 m vertically, and 11.19 ns in timing, with the actual solution errors falling well within these bounds.
item.dc:creator: Samuel C. Morgan, Zacharias M. Komodromos, Wenkai Qin, Andrew Graff, Zachary L. Clements, W. Jeremy Morrison, Todd E. Humphreys

item.title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.13766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.
item.dc:creator: Santosh Mohan Rajkumar, Debdipta Goswami, Stephanie Stockar

item.title: Neuromodulation Through Intrinsic Noise
item.description: arXiv:2611.13780v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neuromodulation, the modulation of excitability through the regulation of neuronal parameters, is a key tool in neuromorphic control design. This paper investigates how spiking excitability can be modulated by intrinsic noise. Focusing on a simplified memristive neuron model, we show that intrinsic noise plays distinct functional roles depending on the feedback pathways: Intrinsic noise in the fast excitatory feedback shapes the nature of excitability and modulates the sensitivity of the neuron to external/internal stimuli, whereas that in the slow inhibitory feedback provides internal stimuli that can trigger stochastic spiking. We expect these findings to guide the design of neuromorphic systems that harness intrinsic noise to exploit beneficial stochastic phenomena, such as stochastic resonance.
item.dc:creator: Sunghyun Koo, Jin Gyu Lee, Rodolphe Sepulchre

item.title: Optimal Last-Iterate Bounds for Nonexpansive Stochastic Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2611.13846v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish last-iterate mean-square residual bounds for nonexpansive stochastic approximation (SA), or stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann (KM) iterations. In particular, we consider fixed-point mappings that are nonexpansive with respect to the Euclidean norm, and focus on polynomially decaying stepsizes. We study three conditions on the conditional second moment of the noise, and obtain bounds that are optimal up to logarithmic factors in each case. When it scales linearly with the squared residual, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1-\epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon>0$. In this case, for all considered stepsizes, our bounds match those of the noiseless KM iteration. When it is bounded by a constant, the best rate is $O(\log^2 k/\sqrt{k})$. When it scales affinely with the squared norm of the iterate, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1/2-\epsilon})$, and the mean-square residual can diverge if the stepsizes are not square-summable. Thus, unlike for contractive SA, square-summable stepsizes are necessary for nonexpansive SA. We demonstrate how various algorithms with cocoercive maps, such as stochastic gradient descent, linear SA, and learning in cocoercive games, fit into our framework, and how the different noise conditions arise in each of them.
item.dc:creator: Ramanan Tamizholi, Siddharth Chandak, Rahul Singh

item.title: Learn-To-Propagate: Distributionally Robust Motion Planning for Nonlinear Uncertain Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.13863v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose \emph{Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest)}, a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for \emph{nonlinear} stochastic systems with \emph{unknown} initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system's state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete. Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Figueiredo, Adrien Banse, Qi Heng Ho, Raphael Jungers, Morteza Lahijanian, Luca Laurenti

item.title: The Role of Insurance in Power-System Risk Management: A Critical Review
item.description: arXiv:2611.13909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern power systems are becoming more renewable-rich, digitalized, and interconnected, making risk propagation and economic consequences increasingly complex. Physical mitigation remains the primary means of risk control, but technical and economic limits leave residual risk. Insurance can complement these measures by transferring associated economic losses and influencing power-system decisions through risk-responsive terms. Despite growing interest, the literature remains fragmented across power-system engineering, actuarial science, and risk finance. This review develops an integrated physical-financial perspective for reviewing insurance in power systems. It examines how power system risks generate residual economic losses and the conditions under which these losses can be insured and transferred. It then develops an actuarial framework for insured-loss assessment and pricing. Insurance-aware decision-making is synthesized through four coupling levels describing how financial protection interacts with power-system decisions. Further progress is constrained by weak physical-financial loss validation, incomplete representation of systemic and evolving portfolio risk, and limited empirical and actuarial grounding of insurance-decision feedback. Research priorities include stronger physical-financial data linkage, forward-looking portfolio assessment, multi-timescale decision feedback, and empirical validation. Addressing these priorities would help move power-system insurance from fragmented applications toward a more coherent approach to residual-risk management in future power systems.
item.dc:creator: Jing Huang, Jiale Guo, Chenjia Gu, Chengcheng Shao, Yue Xiang, Tao Qian, Alexis Pengfei Zhao, Xiuli Wang, Junyong Liu, Xifan Wang

item.title: Safe and Scalable Minimax Adaptive Control of Positive Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.14021v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper studies minimax adaptive control of positive linear systems with fixed unknown dynamics and nonnegative disturbances. We reformulate the problem by compressing the historical data into a vector and a positivity-induced consistency set containing the models compatible with the observations. Together with the physical state, these quantities form a sufficient information state and yield an exact reformulation as a standard minimax dynamic game. We allow the admissible input set to adapt to the current consistency set, ensuring positivity for every remaining feasible model. As inconsistent models are eliminated, the input set can expand, allowing less cautious control actions. For finite model sets, we derive an explicit solution to the Bellman inequality and construct a safe and stabilizing certainty-equivalence controller with robustness guarantees. The framework also accommodates structured classes of continuum model uncertainty whose consistency sets admit fixed, finite-dimensional representations, enabling scalable information-state updates.
item.dc:creator: Fethi Bencherki, David Ohlin, Tomas Meijer

item.title: Discrete-Time Stochastic Control Beyond i.i.d. Noise
item.description: arXiv:2611.14088v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study discrete-time stochastic control problems where the noise driving the state dynamics is a stationary infinite-order chain rather than an i.i.d. sequence. We formulate the problem as a controlled Markov process by enlarging the state space to include the posterior distribution of the noise given the state-action history. Assuming that the sensitivity of the noise transition kernel to past noise values decays exponentially, we show that the expected total variation distance between the full-history and finite-memory noise filters decays at rate $\sqrt{N}\rho^{\sqrt{N}}$. We use this result to construct finite-memory control models and establish explicit near-optimality bounds for their policies. Finally, under suitable ergodicity conditions, we show that Q-learning converges to the optimal solution of the approximate model, so the same performance bounds apply to the learned policies.
item.dc:creator: Reyajul Hasan Leon, Ali Devran Kara

item.title: Koopman Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.14186v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a Koopman model-based reinforcement learning (K-MBRL) algorithm for controlling nonlinear robotic systems with unknown dynamics. The K-MBRL learns a control policy by minimizing an approximate policy objective that combines the analytical immediate cost with an estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step predicted state. To this end, we develop a stochastic Koopman operator-based learning method to approximate the unknown nonlinear dynamics in a linear representation, while a critic function estimates the remaining future cost. This formulation offers two key advantages. First, the linear Koopman dynamics simplify the model-dependent policy gradient computation to a constant matrix product, enabling computationally efficient policy improvement. Second, one-step model propagation mitigates the accumulation of prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts while retaining long-term cost information through the critic. The learned policy enables real-time control through feedforward evaluation without online optimization. We establish policy learning convergence guarantees under standard stochastic approximation assumptions. Simulations on HalfCheetah and quadruped four-legged locomotion tasks demonstrate strong sample efficiency and improved performance compared with classical model-free and model-based reinforcement learning baselines. A pendulum swing-up task is used to assess policy gradient approximation accuracy and conduct ablation studies on the learning mechanism and key hyperparameters. The proposed K-MBRL is further validated on a physical quadruped robot performing a challenging sequence of maneuvers: rising to an upright posture supported by two rounded rear feet, maintaining balance during bipedal walking, and safely returning to the ground, as shown in Fig.1.
item.dc:creator: Wenjian Hao, Paulo C. Heredia, Shaoshuai Mou

item.title: Reliable and explainable analysis of AVS/RS by Statistical Model Checking and Process Mining
item.description: arXiv:2611.14371v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated Vehicle Storage and Retrieval Systems (AVS/RS) are increasingly adopted to boost warehouse throughput while containing operational costs. We present an integrated analysis framework that couples discrete-event simulation with Statistical Model Checking (SMC) and Process Mining (PM) to quantify and explain AVS/RS performance. SMC, implemented through the MultiVeStA tool, delivers statistically reliable estimates of key indicators, such as cycle times, throughput, and storage utilization, across alternative stocking and picking policies with user-specified confidence levels. MultiVeStA orchestrates multiple independent simulations in a black-box manner, enabling automated verification. PM ingests the resulting event logs to uncover the behavioral patterns and bottlenecks that drive those indicators, closing the interpretability gap typical of simulation studies. We instantiate the framework on a new open-source AVS/RS simulator configured according to recent industrial guidelines and evaluate multiple control strategies. Results show that the joint use of SMC and PM enables both predictive what-if analyses and post-hoc diagnostics, providing the first combined SMC+PM assessment of AVS/RS operations and a reusable toolchain for automated warehousing research.
item.dc:creator: Emanuele Guerrazzi, Andrea Vandin

item.title: Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Offline Reinforcement Learning with Online Action Selection Enabled by Sparse Gaussian-Process Critics
item.description: arXiv:2611.14374v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data. In its original implementation, the online objective combines the predicted return from a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. We examine the effect of this penalty and replace the critic and AAE with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic. Actions maximise $\mu - \kappa\sigma$, an uncertainty-adjusted estimate of the return from one action followed by the historical operating practice. On the HOFLON polymerisation-reactor benchmark, removing the AAE from HOFLON led to 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs over five critics. At its published weight, the variation in the AAE penalty is four orders of magnitude smaller than the variation in the tree-ensemble critic. Nevertheless, it changes actions when the predicted returns of competing candidates are nearly equal, and paired runs with and without the penalty diverged from the first move. With a Mat\'ern-5/2 sGP critic, $\kappa = 0$ led to failure in 13 of 15 runs, whereas with $\kappa = 3$ none of 15 runs (five critics, three noise realisations) failed. The median and lowest returns were 13,464 and 13,398 (HOFLON: 13,393 and 12,411). A squared-exponential sGP critic with learned inducing inputs needed $\kappa \geq 3$ to remain within the empirical data support in steady state, and then settled with a temperature offset of 2.0 K.
item.dc:creator: Marco Chan (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering, Department of Chemical Engineering, Imperial College London), Christos Evripidou (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering, Department of Chemical Engineering, Imperial College London), Liqiu Dong (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering, Department of Chemical Engineering, Imperial College London), Benoit Chachuat (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering, Department of Chemical Engineering, Imperial College London), Mehmet Mercang\"oz (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering, Department of Chemical Engineering, Imperial College London)

item.title: The Phantom of Davis-Wielandt Shell: A Unified Perspective for Graphical Stability Analysis of MIMO LTI Systems
item.description: arXiv:2507.19918v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a unified perspective based on Davis-Wielandt (DW) shell of linear subspaces for graphical stability analysis of multi-input and multi-output linear time-invariant feedback systems. Connections between DW shells and various graphical representations, as well as gain and phase measures, are established through an intuitive geometric perspective. We establish a strict DW separation theorem which characterizes subspace separation and provides a basis for comparing the implications and relative conservatism of graphical separation conditions. In particular, we introduce the rotated scaled relative graph ($\theta$-SRG) and show that its separation is equivalent to DW shell separation and is therefore the least conservative among all the graphical conditions considered. We derive pointwise and boundary stability conditions for bi-component feedback interconnections and establish a weak DW separation result that relaxes the strict separation requirement at open-loop poles. We also discuss applications to robust stability analysis and provide a numerical example illustrating how DW shells serve as a more reliable robustness indicator.
item.dc:creator: Ding Zhang, Xiaokan Yang, Axel Ringh, Li Qiu

item.title: Event-Based Control via Sparsity-Promoting Regularization: A Rollout Approach with Performance Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2509.24799v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a controller design framework aiming to balance control performance and actuation rate. Control performance is evaluated by an infinite-horizon average cost, and the number of control actions is penalized via sparsity-promoting regularization. Since the formulated optimal control problem has a combinatorial nature, we employ a rollout algorithm to obtain a tractable suboptimal solution. In the proposed scheme, actuation timings are determined through a multistage minimization procedure based on a receding-horizon approach, and the corresponding control inputs are computed online. We establish theoretical performance guarantees with respect to periodic control and prove the stability of the closed-loop system. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through a numerical example.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 2026 American Control Conference (ACC), pp. 4590-4595, 2026
item.dc:creator: Shumpei Nishida, Kunihisa Okano

item.title: Explicit MPC for the constrained zonotope case with low-rank matrix updates
item.description: arXiv:2511.02433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Solving the explicit Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem requires enumerating all critical regions and their associated feedback laws, a task that scales exponentially with the system dimension and the prediction horizon, as well. When the problem's constraints are boxes or zonotopes, the feasible domain admits a compact constrained-zonotope representation. Building on this insight, we exploit the geometric properties of the equivalent constrained-zonotope reformulation to accelerate the computation of the explicit solution. Specifically, we formulate the multi-parametric problem in the lifted generator space and solve it using second-order optimality conditions, employ low-rank matrix updates to reduce computation time, and introduce an analytic enumeration of candidate active sets that yields the explicit solution in tree form.
item.dc:creator: Stefan S. Mihai, Florin Stoican, Martin Monnigmann, Bogdan D. Ciubotaru

item.title: Stability of DC Microgrids with Nested Nonlinear Control Frameworks: The Fast Communication Scenario
item.description: arXiv:2511.10401v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As modern power systems continue to evolve into multi-agent, converter-dominated systems that demand reliable, stable, and optimal control architectures within an expandable framework, this paper investigates scalable stability guarantees of a promising nonlinear communication-reliant control framework for DC microgrids. Particularly, relying on nested control loops, inner decentralized (primary) and outer distributed (secondary), the control configurations are designed to simultaneously achieve proportional current sharing and voltage containment within pre-specified limits, at the converged steady state. By enforcing sufficient time-scale separation at the border between the control loops, the system admits a singular perturbation formulation, allowing global exponential stability (G.E.S.) to be established via Lyapunov arguments. Although the theoretical G.E.S. certificate is structurally scalable, the stability guarantees depend on a sufficiently large permanent leakage, introduced in the primary controller. Thus, this paper emphasizes the importance of appropriate practical tuning guidelines for establishing suitable system configurations under which the DC microgrid is practically scalable and its equilibrium is G.E.S.. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through case studies on a low-voltage DC microgrid under load variations and topological changes, followed by a small-signal stability analysis
item.dc:creator: Cornelia Skaga, Mahdieh S. Sadabadi, Gilbert Bergna-Diaz

item.title: Configuration-Constrained Tube MPC for Periodic Operation
item.description: arXiv:2512.04239v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Periodic operation often emerges as the economically optimal mode in industrial processes subject to varying economic or environmental conditions. This paper proposes a robust model predictive control (MPC) framework for uncertain systems described by polytopic linear difference inclusions (LDIs), whose dynamics evolve as convex combinations of finitely many linear control systems subject to additive disturbances. The robust control problem is formulated as a convex optimization program over configuration-constrained polytopic tubes, with the objective of tracking a periodic tube that is optimal for a given economic criterion. Artificial variables embedded in the formulation ensure recursive feasibility and robust constraint satisfaction under changes in the economic criterion, and convergence to the optimal periodic tube when the criterion remains constant. To improve computational efficiency, we introduce a quadratic upper approximation of the periodic cost under a Lipschitz continuity assumption, yielding a Quadratic Program (QP) that preserves the above theoretical guarantees. The approach is demonstrated on an illustrative example and an eight-state ball--plate system.
item.dc:creator: Filippo Badalamenti, Jose A. Borja-Conde, Sampath Kumar Mulagaleti, Boris Houska, Alberto Bemporad, Mario Eduardo Villanueva

item.title: Neural Network-Enhanced Frequency-Constrained Optimal Power Flow With Worst RoCoF and Frequency Deviation
item.description: arXiv:2602.11063v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frequency-constrained optimal power flow (FCOPF) should keep the rate of change of frequency (RoCoF) and the frequency deviation (FD) within their limits after a specified generator out-age. The linearized frequency constraints commonly used in FCOPF are derived from aggregated system frequency response (SFR) models, which describe the center of inertia (COI) fre-quency with simplified governor dynamics and can underesti-mate the frequency excursions experienced by individual genera-tors. To address this issue, this paper develops a neural network-based frequency predictor (NN-FP) trained on electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations in PSCAD/EMTDC. The NN-FP predicts the worst RoCoF and the worst FD over the monitored generators, namely the generators at all buses other than the contingency bus. The trained NN-FP is reformulated and embed-ded into FCOPF with tightened frequency limits obtained from the test set prediction errors of NN-FP, leading to the proposed NN-FCOPF. The proposed model is compared with a traditional optimal power flow and a linearized FCOPF. EMT validation of 24-hour dispatches on the IEEE 9-bus and 39-bus systems shows that NN-FCOPF satisfies both limits in all hourly cases for the specified contingency, whereas the linearized FCOPF violates the limits in some hours because it underestimates the worst genera-tor RoCoF and FD.
item.dc:creator: Fan Jiang, Xingpeng Li, Pascal Van Hentenryck

item.title: Distributed Event-Triggered Consensus Control of Discrete-Time Linear Multi-Agent Systems under LQ Performance Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2603.25161v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper proposes a distributed event-triggered control method that not only guarantees consensus of multi-agent systems but also satisfies a given LQ performance constraint. Taking the standard distributed control scheme with all-time communication as a baseline, we consider the problem of designing an event-triggered communication rule such that the resulting LQ cost satisfies a performance constraint with respect to the baseline cost while consensus is achieved. The main difficulty is that the performance requirement is global, whereas triggering decisions are made locally and asynchronously by individual agents, which cannot directly evaluate the global performance degradation. To address this issue, we decompose allowable degradation across agents and design a triggering rule that uses only locally available information to satisfy the given LQ performance constraint. For general linear agents on an undirected graph, we derive a sufficient condition that guarantees both consensus and the prescribed performance level. We also develop a tractable offline design method for the triggering parameters. Numerical examples illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Shumpei Nishida, Kunihisa Okano

item.title: Spurious-Free Lithium Niobate Bulk Acoustic Wave Resonator with Grounded-Ring Electrode
item.description: arXiv:2604.06426v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-performance piezoelectric resonators are promising energy-storage elements for piezoelectric power conversion because of their compact footprint and low loss at frequencies where conventional magnetic components become bulky and inefficient. However, their practical use is often limited by the trade-off between a high electromechanical coupling coefficient ($k^2$) for wide-band operation and the emergence of spurious acoustic modes that limit the resonators' inductive bandwidth. This work reports a spurious-free thickness-extensional (TE)-mode bulk acoustic wave (BAW) resonator in single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) based on a grounded-ring electrode architecture. The proposed structure is analyzed through simulation and experimentally validated using electrical characterization and laser Doppler vibrometry (LDV). The results show that the grounded ring modifies the effective boundary conditions of the acoustic device, enabling a piston-like modal response that suppresses lateral spurious modes across the inductive band. The demonstrated device operates at 10.14 MHz and achieves an electromechanical coupling coefficient of 29.6%, a maximum in-band Bode quality factor ($Q_\textit{Bode}$) of 5230, and a figure of merit (FoM, $Q\cdot k^2$) of 1548. These results establish the grounded-ring TE-mode LN BAW resonator as a practical platform for piezoelectric power conversion and a broader design approach for realizing high-performance spurious-free acoustic resonators.
item.dc:creator: Vakhtang Chulukhadze, Kristi Nguyen, Eric Stolt, Kilian Shambaugh, Weston Braun, Tzu-Hsuan Hsu, Osama Jameel, Juan Rivas-Davila, Ruochen Lu

item.title: Data-driven Linear Quadratic Integral Control: A Convex Formulation and Policy Gradient Approach
item.description: arXiv:2604.14905v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the data-driven synthesis of linear quadratic integral (LQI) controllers for continuous-time systems. The objective is to achieve optimal state-feedback control with integral action for reference tracking using only measured data. To this end, we derive a data-driven closed-loop parameterization of the augmented dynamics that incorporates the integral state while relying solely on input-state-output measurements of the underlying system. Based on this parameterization, a data-driven convex optimization problem is formulated whose solution yields the optimal linear quadratic regulator (LQR) feedback gain for the augmented system without explicit knowledge of the system matrices. In addition, a projected policy gradient flow, which is a preconditioned version of the model-based policy gradient flow, is derived to compute the optimal controller within the space of stabilizing gains. The proposed approach enables data-driven optimal tracking control while avoiding explicit state augmentation in the data collection phase. For time-varying gains, as they arise in an online implementation, the direct, incremental, and feedforward realizations of the LQI controller are compared, and the equilibrium required for feedforward is obtained from the same data. The method is illustrated on a distributed generation unit (DGU) in a DC microgrid, including an online implementation with closed-loop data under load changes, and by a Monte Carlo study on random systems with noisy data.
item.dc:creator: Armin Gie{\ss}ler, Pol Jan\'e-Soneira, S\"oren Hohmann

item.title: An extended Perron-Frobenius operator filter for nonlinear state estimation
item.description: arXiv:2607.26632v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose an extended Perron--Frobenius Operator Filter (PFOF) for nonlinear state estimation. The method learns the Perron--Frobenius operator, an infinite-dimensional linear operator fully preserving properties of a nonlinear dynamical system, using the extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (eDMD). This enables us to explicitly account for non-Gaussian distributions exhibited by the nonlinear system within a linear-operator representation, while retaining the freedom to choose basis functions in eDMD. Through two numerical examples, we show that the extended PFOF achieves high computational efficiency and high estimation accuracy by exploiting the flexibility in the choice of basis functions in eDMD.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Miwa, Yoshihiko Susuki, Shunji Kotsuki

item.title: Industrial Load Modeling and Optimization for Market-Based Interaction with Power Systems
item.description: arXiv:2608.15076v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The transition toward a renewable-dominated power system increases the flexibility needed to balance net-load variations. Industrial loads account for over 40% of the world's electricity consumption and can shift large amounts of demand through automated production scheduling. However, making industrial processes a dependable flexibility resource for power systems remains challenging because industrial process constraints are non-convex, equipment parameters are often private, and device-level models of thousands of facilities are too detailed for aggregator and power-system optimization. This dissertation builds computationally efficient methods for modeling and optimizing industrial flexibility for power-system interaction. Specifically, this dissertation uses smart meters as the external measurement interface and maps industrial process constraints into a concise flexibility space for power-system operation. The resulting chain of mechanism modeling, parameter identification, constraint dimension reduction, and optimal decision-making makes industrial-load participation computationally tractable while retaining precise process models for final execution.
item.dc:creator: Ruike Lyu

item.title: Formal Synthesis of Robust Koopman-Model Predictive Control: A Case Study in AC-DC Power Conversion
item.description: arXiv:2609.15197v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This letter proposes a formal synthesis of Robust Koopman-Model Predictive Control (RK-MPC), a novel data-driven approach to formal synthesis of systems with nonlinear dynamics. We formulate a novel optimization problem for RK-MPC by incorporating specifications described by Signal Temporal Logic and prove its closed-loop performance. Effectiveness of the proposed RK-MPC is evaluated by applying it to the reliable design of an AC-DC power converter.
item.dc:creator: Shun Hirose, Shiu Mochiyama, Yoshihiko Susuki

item.title: Holonic Graceful Transitions Across Centralized, Decentralized, Distributed, and Local Control in DER-rich Cyber-Power Distribution System
item.description: arXiv:2609.27759v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) in distribution system necessitates adaptive coordination frameworks. These frameworks must remain optimal during normal operation and resilient under cyber physical disturbances. Existing coordinated control approaches are typically deployed as static architectures with limited ability to adapt when communication degrades, local instability emerges, and operating conditions become spatially heterogeneous. This work addresses the gap by proposing a DER service-independent edge autonomous holonic adaptive coordination framework. In this framework, each DER controller executes its own control actions and transitions among centralized, distributed, decentralized, and local autonomous coordination modes without always relying on static coordination commands from the grid operator. The framework preserves coordination continuity across modes by retaining local controller states while reconfiguring only the coordination topology, information exchange pattern, and fallback action associated with the active DER service. Graceful transitions are enabled through dwell timers, rate limiting, and safety overrides to prevent dynamic instability during mode changes. Volt VAR control is used as a representative distribution automation application to validate the proposed architecture in a cyber-physical Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testbed. The proposed approach is evaluated under diverse cyber-physical event-based scenarios, showing region-confined adaptation under localized disturbance, reduced coordination traffic during coordination switching, and node-confined mitigation under cyber attack through edge anomaly detection and neighbor-corroborated impact estimation.
item.dc:creator: Md Fazley Rafy, Niloy Patari, Anurag K. Srivastava

item.title: Computationally Constrained First-Order Prediction-Correction Approach for Time-Varying Convex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.38820v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time-varying optimization methods often predict the locations of time-varying optima, then sample the objective function being minimized, and then compute corrections to those predictions. However, existing methods typically do not account for settings in which the number of computations is limited. Therefore, in this work we formulate a prediction-correction algorithm that is designed to obey a budget constraint on the total number of iterations it can execute over a given time horizon. We first identify a threshold on the average number of computations between samples of the objective, above which a bound from prior work certifies contraction of iterates toward a minimizer. Below this threshold, we introduce a finite-horizon contraction certificate, which we use to give budget conditions under which the tracking error admits an explicit bound that decays at a prescribed rate. We also present an algorithm to determine how many prediction and correction steps should be executed for each sample of the objective, while obeying a given budget on the allowable number of computations. Empirically, we show in a simulation that our approach reduces cumulative tracking error by 45.5 % relative to a comparable baseline approach.
item.dc:creator: Negin Musavi, Oscar Jed R. Chuy, Melkior Ornik, Matthew T. Hale

item.title: A Global Routing Method for Electronic Circuit Design Integrating Flow Matching and Constrained A*
item.description: arXiv:2611.02304v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Global routing is a fundamental issue in the design of electronic circuits, as it directly relates to the efficiency, reliability, and compactness of the overall layout of integrated systems. As the demand for higher functionality and reliability within a limited chip area increases, the importance of routing as a design consideration has never been greater. Efficient global routing optimization techniques are therefore required to connect all pins with minimal wirelength (WL), while avoiding congestion and interference across multiple nets within the design space. As the number of nets to be routed increases, global routing inherently suffers from a combinatorial explosion in the design space, making it increasingly difficult to obtain feasible solutions. In this paper, we focus on solving constrained global routing problems based on a heuristic A*-based framework. Based on this concept, a hybrid approach is proposed by integrating constrained A* with flow matching (FM). The method utilizes FM to construct a global cost map that captures routing tendencies across the design space, which is then used to guide the constrained A* search process. This enables efficient exploration of the solution space while satisfying routing constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable WL and via usage to baseline methods while maintaining constraint satisfaction across a wide range of scenarios. Notably, the framework shows strong capability in solving complex routing instances that are difficult to handle using conventional approaches. Additionally, the method shows robust generalization performance across different problem sizes and net configurations.
item.dc:creator: Sanghoon Jin, Sumin Lee, Namwoo Kang

item.title: Predictive Neuromorphic Control of a Scanning Mirror System: An Event-Centric Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.11634v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Organizing control around events can reduce sensing and actuation demands while directly linking control decisions to the occurrence and timing of desired system behaviors. This paper proposes a novel event-centric model predictive control (MPC) framework that unifies event sensing, event prediction, and event regulation. Events define the feedback information, prediction horizon, and event-timing objectives, placing them at the center of predictive control design. The framework is developed for a scanning mirror system equipped with a baseline neuromorphic controller composed of spiking neurons that supports sparse actuation. The control objective is to achieve prescribed zero-crossing times and a desired scanning range while minimizing the mechanical energy transferred between the actuator and the mirror. A sampling-based algorithm is presented to obtain suboptimal solutions of the event-centric MPC optimization problem without requiring an explicit event-to-event prediction model. By grounding predictive optimization in events, the proposed framework opens a new direction for MPC design and its integration with neuromorphic control.
item.dc:creator: Changrui Liu, Robin Wroblowski, Anil Alan, Shengling Shi, Rodolphe Sepulchre, Bart De Schutter

item.title: Safe Approximate Nonlinear Model Predictive Control Without Expert Demonstrations
item.description: arXiv:2603.24503v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Repeated online optimization makes nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) computationally demanding for real-time applications. Neural approximations reduce this cost but often require large datasets of expert NMPC solutions. We introduce Sequential Approximate MPC (Seq-AMPC), a label-free recurrent framework that generates complete control sequences along predicted trajectories using parameters shared across the prediction horizon. The policy is trained directly through known dynamics with losses for control cost, constraint satisfaction, and a cost-decrease condition aligned with a feasible-backup safety filter. Building on this filter, we introduce a stage-cost-dependent acceptance tolerance that preserves recursive feasibility, constraint satisfaction, and asymptotic convergence under nominal MPC assumptions, independently of neural approximation error. We further derive Hoeffding-based finite-sample bounds for the expected fraction of applied proposals and closed-loop cost discrepancy relative to NMPC. We evaluate Seq-AMPC on a quadcopter, chain of masses, obstacle-avoidance vehicle, and robotic manipulator, comparing recurrent and feedforward policies under label-free and imitation training. Across four benchmarks, training takes 0.2-1.7 GPU hours per policy without expert control labels. The filtered controller applies 97.2-99.1% of neural proposals and achieves mean closed-loop cost ratios within 0.3% of NMPC on jointly completed episodes. Tests with suboptimal feasible initial plans further demonstrate the benefit of neural replanning.
item.dc:creator: Mihaela-Larisa Clement, M\'onika Farsang, Johannes Edelmann, Manfred Pl\"ochl, Radu Grosu, Ezio Bartocci, Agnes Poks, Luca Marzari

item.title: Discounted MPC and infinite-horizon optimal control under plant-model mismatch: Stability and suboptimality
item.description: arXiv:2604.08521v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the robustness to plant-model mismatch of nonlinear systems in closed loop with (discounted) optimal controllers designed for a nominal model, with quadratic stage costs across finite and infinite horizons. By combining Lyapunov analysis with a unifying relaxed dynamic programming framework, we establish conditions that guarantee robust stability alongside improved suboptimality bounds compared to existing literature. A key step in our analysis is proving that stability counteracts time-accumulated error growth due to plant-model mismatch, yielding robustness bounds that hold uniformly across all prediction horizons.
item.dc:creator: Robert H. Moldenhauer, Karl Worthmann, Romain Postoyan, Dragan Ne\v{s}i\'c, Mathieu Granzotto

item.title: Adaptive Reparametrized Time for Score-Based Diffusion Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2607.02137v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.
item.dc:creator: Yilie Huang, Wenpin Tang, Xun Yu Zhou

item.title: Feedback Stabilization for Sampled Linear Systems with Control-linear Noise
item.description: arXiv:2609.30438v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we consider linear stochastic systems with control-linear noise and periodically sampled measurements. We address the problem of feedback stabilization in the mean-square sense. The main contribution of the paper is to provide a necessary and sufficient condition for feedback stabilization. In particular, we relate feedback stabilizability of the stochastic system to the existence of a fixed point of a Riccati-type algebraic equation and, further, to the existence of a solution to an infinite-horizon optimal control problem.
item.dc:creator: Cynthia Cheng, Xudong Chen

item.title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.35658v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56,202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2,000 reports, the chains recover 90.8% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1,205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.
item.dc:creator: Yutian Pang, Yifang Tian, Xinyu Zhao, Jueming Hu, John-Paul Clarke, Hans-Arno Jacobsen

item.title: Computing GR(1) Assume-Guarantee Contracts
item.description: arXiv:2610.37534v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Assume-guarantee contracts provide a set of algebraic operations that enable the efficient compositional design and analysis of complex engineering systems. The explicit computation of these operations at component interfaces is currently supported only for some logics lacking a notion of time. This paper develops theory and algorithms to compute these operations when the contracts are expressed in the GR(1) modulo theory. The key challenge is the computation of two quantifier elimination problems for temporal formulas. We develop context-aided variable elimination procedures on GR(1)-modulo formulas, establish their soundness, characterize subproblem-wise optimal solutions within an admissible class of formulas, and use the procedures to compute contract operations, including composition and quotient. We implement the resulting framework in Pacti, automating compositional reasoning over GR(1) contracts. Finally, we demonstrate the framework on an automated emergency-braking case study, where we compute system-level contracts and expose compatibility conditions arising from the interaction of component specifications. Experiments on synthetic families show that the cost is governed by the number of eliminated variables and liveness conjuncts, and a comparison with exact automata-based elimination shows complementary scaling.

item.title: Delay-Certified Readiness Barriers for Overactuated Multirotor Allocation Without Lipschitz Constants
item.description: arXiv:2611.03490v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Overactuated multirotors can produce the same wrench with many rotor-speed combinations, some of which leave the vehicle unable to change its wrench quickly, e.g., to reject a gust. Readiness barriers keep this ability, the readiness, above a floor, but only in continuous time; with sampled commands and varying speed-controller delays, the available robustness bound covers less than one millisecond. We remove this limit by exploiting the structure of the problem: each rotor responds monotonically and in closed form to its own torque, so the speeds reachable under uncertain switching times lie in a cheaply computed box, and the lowest readiness over that box sits at a corner known in advance. This yields a Lipschitz-free test that a command keeps the readiness above its floor until the next sample, plus a fallback torque that keeps the vehicle on a certified plan. In hexarotor simulations with 2--40~ms delays and $\pm2$~ms jitter, the filter never violated the floor. At $10\pm2$~ms, it matched a delay-compensating predictor within the design envelope and cost 2--30\% more tracking error beyond it, where the predictor alone violated the floor in 2 to 16 of 16 missions. A tuned robust predictor was also safe with synchronous switching, but not with per-rotor jitter.

item.title: Mass Scaling Laws for Energy-Optimal Horizontal Multirotor Flight
item.description: arXiv:2611.04748v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multicopters are a type of aerial robot seeing extensive real-world applications but with range and endurance as critical bottlenecks. Optimization of its energy efficiency through energy-aware flight planning (e.g. cruise speed-scheduling) has hence been an important topic. The mass of the multicopter is an important factor to consider, as it has a significant impact on efficiency, and many common applications are subject to frequent mass variation due to payload change. This work derives closed-form scaling relationships between the energy-optimal steady horizontal flight behavior of a multicopter and its vehicle mass, and validates them experimentally on two multirotor platforms. Specifically, for mass-only variation, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show through a combination of numerical simulation, theoretical derivation, and experimental validation that (1) the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of vehicle mass; (2) the energy-optimal pitch angle is constant with respect to mass; and (3) the optimal energy per meter is proportional to mass. The analysis shows that these three relationships arise from a common mass-similarity property of the steady-state flight and rotor-aerodynamic equations. Furthermore, the obtained scaling relationships enable simple yet effective cruise-speed planning to optimize energy efficiency and extend the range and endurance of the multicopter.

item.title: PA-SaR: Perception-Aware Learning, Control, and Coordination for Multi-Robot Search and Rescue
item.description: arXiv:2611.11648v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.
